# Community spatial continuity is redundant across species rather than generated by turnover in small-mammal metacommunities

## One-sentence result

Across 16 prospectively selected NEON sites, pooling target small-mammal species never increased multiscale spatial continuity beyond the best individual species; instead, 13 sites contained multiple species that independently reproduced complete community-level continuity.

## Abstract

Species turnover can allow different taxa to occupy complementary parts of a heterogeneous landscape, suggesting that a community might be spatially more continuous than any of its constituent species. We tested this idea prospectively using NSF NEON small-mammal box-trapping data. Sixteen previously unopened sites were selected using response-blind trap geometry only. At each site, we defined a small set of multiscale spatial neighbourhood graphs and measured continuity as the fraction of graphs in which every occupied trap had at least one occupied peer within the corresponding neighbourhood. We compared the pooled target-species community with each constituent species and defined emergent connectivity gain as community continuity minus the maximum single-species continuity. To separate spatial species turnover from richness and composition, we permuted complete local assemblages among the fixed community-positive traps, preserving every species' occupancy frequency, the multiset of local richness values, and within-trap species co-occurrence. All 16 sites were scorable. The preregistered turnover hypothesis was rejected: median emergent gain was zero, no site had a positive null-adjusted gain, and the one-sided sign test gave p=1.0. At every site, at least one individual species was fully continuous across all spatial neighbourhood graphs, and 13 of 16 sites contained two or more such species. Across sites, 32 different species appeared among the fully continuous species, while no species filled that role at more than three sites. Fifteen pooled communities were also fully continuous, while at ORNL taxonomic pooling reduced continuity from 1.0 for the best individual species to 0.25 for the pooled guild. No site contained a spatial scale at which the pooled guild remained continuous while every individual species failed. Heterospecific-only local rescue was rare (median 0.27% of supported node-scale targets; maximum 6.6%). Exploratorily, species-rich sites contained more individually fully continuous species (Spearman rho=0.668), but the fraction of eligible species that were fully continuous showed no positive richness trend (rho=-0.159, p=0.555). These results indicate occupancy-continuity redundancy: community continuity was repeatedly supplied by multiple constituent species rather than emerging from turnover among spatially restricted species.

## 1. Introduction

Ecologists often expect species turnover to create complementarity across heterogeneous landscapes. Different taxa can dominate different environments, and their spatial replacement can stabilize ecosystem properties across space. This logic underlies spatial-insurance theory and more broadly the metacommunity idea that regional biodiversity can maintain properties that no local population can provide alone.

A similar intuition can be applied to spatial occurrence patterns. If individual species occupy different parts of a landscape, pooling them might fill gaps in species-specific distributions and create a community-level pattern that is more spatially continuous than any one species. This possibility matters for community connectivity, biodiversity monitoring and conservation planning, because community-level maps are often constructed by aggregating species whose individual spatial structures differ.

However, taxonomic pooling need not create new continuity. A community can appear continuous because one species is already continuous, or because several different species independently reproduce the same community-level continuity. We refer to the latter pattern as occupancy-continuity redundancy: multiple species separately satisfy the same spatial continuity criterion, without implying functional equivalence or identical ecological roles. Conversely, pooling can reduce continuity when a rare or spatially isolated species adds occupied locations that lack nearby occupied peers.

We tested these alternatives prospectively using NEON small-mammal communities. Our primary hypothesis was that species turnover creates emergent community continuity: pooled target-species occurrences should remain continuous across more spatial neighbourhood scales than the best individual species, and this gain should exceed a null in which complete observed local assemblages are randomly relocated among the same occupied traps.

The design distinguishes three ecological outcomes. A positive gain beyond the permutation null supports spatial complementarity. A positive raw gain that is reproduced by the null indicates a richness or composition effect without special spatial arrangement. Zero gain indicates single-species sufficiency, while negative gain indicates a pooling penalty in which added taxa create spatially unsupported community occurrences.

## 2. Methods

### 2.1 Prospective fresh-site design

The analysis was preregistered before biological response access. We used NEON Small mammal box trapping, DP1.10072.001, RELEASE-2026. Sixteen sites used in an earlier methodological programme were excluded, as were three sites whose public response summaries had been viewed during study design.

All remaining sites were ordered by site code. Site selection used only product metadata, trap locations and geometry. The first 16 sites passing the response-blind structural criteria were fixed: JORN, KONA, LAJA, LENO, MLBS, MOAB, NIWO, NOGP, OAES, ONAQ, ORNL, OSBS, RMNP, SERC, SJER and SOAP.

No response endpoint was opened before this roster and all site-level spatial graph fingerprints were frozen.

### 2.2 Target guild and trap locations

The response guild comprised NEON SMALL_MAMMAL taxa classified as species and as target taxa by the protocol taxonomy. Two species whose public species-level summaries had been exposed during earlier design work were excluded prospectively.

The spatial unit was the individual mammal trap. Trap coordinates containing X were excluded before response access because NEON's official small-mammal geolocation implementation treats these locations as uncertain. Target-positive X-coordinate records were counted but did not enter spatial calculations.

### 2.3 Multiscale spatial continuity assay

For each site we calculated Haversine distances among frozen trap coordinates. Distance thresholds were chosen response-blindly to span target largest-connected-component fractions of 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 and 0.90, with finite-node completion where required by the structural adequacy rule. Exact duplicate adjacency graphs were counted once.

For a given species and a given spatial graph, continuity was positive when every occupied trap had at least one other occupied trap connected by an admitted one-step edge. The pooled community was evaluated by replacing the species-specific occupied set with the union of all eligible target-species occurrences.

For each site we calculated the fraction of distinct spatial graphs that passed this criterion for the pooled community and separately for every species observed at at least two traps.

### 2.4 Primary ecological estimand

The preregistered site-level effect was

emergent connectivity gain =
community continuity fraction - maximum single-species continuity fraction.

A positive value means that pooling species produces spatial continuity not achieved by any individual species. Zero means that at least one species fully explains the pooled continuity. Negative values indicate that taxonomic pooling adds spatially unsupported occupied traps and reduces continuity relative to the best individual species.

At least eight scored fresh sites were required.

### 2.5 Assemblage-relocation null

To distinguish species turnover from simple richness or species-frequency effects, we randomized the spatial arrangement of observed local assemblages.

At each site we formed a trap-by-species incidence matrix over community-positive traps. Each permutation reassigned complete incidence rows among those same positive trap coordinates. This preserved exactly:

- the community-positive trap set;
- every species' number of occupied traps;
- the multiset of trap-level species richness values;
- the complete within-trap co-occurrence assemblages.

Only the locations of the local assemblages changed.

We used 999 preregistered permutations per site. The null-adjusted gain was the observed emergent gain minus the median permuted gain. The confirmatory aggregate test was a one-sided exact sign test of positive null-adjusted site effects against probability 0.5. Exact zeros counted as non-positive.

### 2.6 Mechanistic secondary quantities

We also calculated three preregistered secondary quantities.

Strict emergent-world fraction was the fraction of spatial graphs in which the pooled guild was continuous but no eligible individual species was continuous.

Cross-species rescue fraction measured, among pooled positive targets in community-continuous graphs, the fraction that had a positive neighbouring trap but no neighbouring trap sharing any species with the target assemblage.

Dominance coverage was the maximum number of community-positive traps occupied by any one species divided by the number of community-positive traps.

### 2.7 Once-only response access

After the site roster, graph fingerprints, target guild, metrics, null model and decision rule were frozen, one authenticated NEON query was executed. The run consumed 639 response files and 299,965,029 biological-response bytes. All 16 fresh sites were scorable, and no site replacement or response repair was performed.

## 3. Results

### 3.1 Species turnover did not create emergent community continuity

The preregistered primary hypothesis was rejected completely.

Median emergent connectivity gain was 0. No site had a positive null-adjusted gain (0/16), and the one-sided exact sign-test p-value was 1.0.

The spatial relocation null reproduced the observed gains at every site. Thus neither raw community pooling nor the observed spatial arrangement of assemblages produced continuity beyond the best constituent species.

### 3.2 At least one individual species was fully continuous at every site

Maximum single-species continuity was 1.0 at all 16 sites.

The pooled community was also fully continuous at 15 sites. Consequently, the community gain was exactly zero at 15 of 16 sites.

The number of individually fully continuous species ranged from one to eight, with a median of two. Among species occurring at at least two traps, the median fraction that were individually fully continuous was 0.477.

These results show that community continuity was not attributable to a single universal dominant taxon. Thirteen of 16 sites contained at least two individually fully continuous species. Across all sites, 32 species appeared among the fully continuous set, and no species did so at more than three sites. Thus the same community-level spatial property was repeatedly supplied by different constituent species in different metacommunities.

### 3.3 Pooling reduced continuity at ORNL

ORNL was the sole site with a negative emergent gain.

The best individual species had continuity 1.0, whereas the pooled target community had continuity 0.25, producing a gain of -0.75.

Thus adding taxa can decrease community continuity under an all-positive support criterion when additional species introduce occupied traps that are spatially isolated at otherwise supported neighbourhood scales.

### 3.4 Heterospecific rescue was local and rare

No site had a strict emergent spatial graph: the strict emergent-world fraction was zero at all 16 sites.

Cross-species-only rescue occurred at ten sites but was quantitatively small. The median cross-species rescue fraction was 0.0027 and the maximum was 0.066, observed at RMNP.

Local heterospecific neighbourhood support therefore occurred, but it never translated into additional system-level spatial continuity beyond the best species.

### 3.5 Richness was associated with continuity redundancy, not stronger turnover rescue

The 16 sites contained between two and 16 observed target species, with a median of seven. Dominance coverage ranged from 0.501 to 0.982, with a median of 0.835.

In exploratory post hoc analyses using only the frozen site summaries, species richness was positively associated with the number of individually fully continuous species (Spearman rho=0.668, p=0.0047). Richness was negatively associated with dominance coverage (rho=-0.594, p=0.015). Richness was not positively associated with cross-species rescue (rho=-0.390, p=0.135).

Exploratorily, richness increased the absolute number of individually continuous species, but not their proportion among species with at least two occupied traps (rho=-0.159, p=0.555). The pattern is therefore more consistent with accumulation of redundant continuity providers than with a richness-driven increase in the probability that any given species is continuous.

## 4. Discussion

Our prospective test rejected a simple but intuitive metacommunity hypothesis. Pooling species did not create spatial continuity beyond that already achieved by individual small-mammal species. Across 16 fresh NEON sites, at least one constituent species was fully continuous across every declared spatial neighbourhood scale, and no site showed a positive emergent gain.

This result distinguishes redundancy from complementarity. Spatial-insurance arguments emphasize compensation among species occupying different environmental or spatial contexts. We found little evidence for that mechanism in the continuity endpoint tested here. Heterospecific-only neighbourhood rescue existed, but it was rare and never created a spatial scale at which the community succeeded while all individual species failed.

Instead, community continuity was individually sufficient and often occupancy-redundant. The median site contained two species that each independently satisfied all continuity scales; 13 of 16 sites contained at least two, and the role was distributed across 32 species. This suggests a different route by which biodiversity can make a community-level spatial property robust: not by stitching together mutually incomplete species distributions, but by providing multiple taxa that can each independently span the relevant spatial neighbourhoods.

The distinction matters for community connectivity assessment. Community-level connectivity is often motivated by the difficulty of choosing one focal species or by the expectation that different species contribute complementary movement pathways. Our result shows that taxonomic aggregation can instead conceal the fact that the observed community property is already carried by constituent species. In one site, ORNL, aggregation was actively detrimental because sparsely supported occurrences lowered pooled continuity relative to the best species.

We do not infer dispersal mechanisms from these occurrence patterns. The continuity assay identifies whether occupied traps have occupied neighbours under frozen spatial thresholds; it does not estimate movement rates, demographic exchange or causal habitat filtering. Likewise, the richness-redundancy correlations were post hoc and should be treated as mechanism-generating evidence rather than confirmatory causal tests.

The strongest conclusion is narrower but positive. In these fresh small-mammal communities, community-level spatial continuity was a redundant property of constituent species: every site had at least one independently continuous species, most had several, and the identity of those species changed among sites. Turnover among spatially incomplete species was not required to generate the observed community continuity.

## 5. Claim boundary

Supported:
- all 16 fresh sites contained at least one individually fully continuous target species;
- pooling species did not increase continuity at any site;
- no strict turnover-generated continuity was observed;
- heterospecific-only rescue was rare and local;
- taxonomic pooling reduced continuity at one site;
- occupancy-continuity redundancy was widespread: 13/16 sites had multiple independently continuous species, involving 32 species across the full site set;
- exploratory richness patterns favor accumulation of redundant continuity providers over turnover complementarity.

Not supported:
- species turnover is generally unimportant to metacommunities;
- the best continuity species is always the numerically dominant species;
- the post hoc richness-redundancy association is causal;
- continuity fraction is a direct dispersal-rate or gene-flow measure;
- the result generalizes outside NEON target small mammals without new validation.

## 6. Figure plan

Figure 1 — Competing ecological mechanisms.
Panel A: turnover complementarity, where species-specific gaps are filled by other taxa and pooled continuity exceeds every species.
Panel B: single-species sufficiency/redundancy, where one or more species independently span the spatial neighbourhoods.
Panel C: pooling penalty, where adding isolated occurrences reduces pooled continuity.

Figure 2 — Fresh 16-site confirmatory result.
For each site, paired community and best-species continuity fractions. Fifteen sites overlap at 1.0; ORNL shows community 0.25 versus best species 1.0.

Figure 3 — Richness and continuity redundancy.
Target-species richness versus number of individually fully continuous species, explicitly labelled exploratory/post hoc. A second panel shows richness versus dominance coverage.
